paragraphs: This paper studies how quickly a Riemannian gradient method solves principal component analysis. The algorithm is a deterministic version of Krasulina’s method. Although the setting is relatively simple, its convergence rate had remained incompletely understood. The authors analyze how the required optimization effort depends jointly on the spectral gap and the desired accuracy.

Their gap-dependent bound scales as O((1/Δ) log(1/ε)), where Δ is the gap and ε measures objective suboptimality. The analysis applies to any real symmetric matrix. However, when the gap is much smaller than the requested accuracy, this expression no longer gives a tight description. The authors therefore also establish a worst-case rate of O((1/ε) log(1/ε)).

Together, these results yield a tight combined rate of O((1/max{Δ, ε}) log(1/ε)). This explains why an extremely small gap need not dictate the convergence cost at a coarser target accuracy. The analysis also suggests a promising learning-rate choice for stochastic variance-reduced PCA algorithms, and the reported experiments support the theoretical findings.
neurips-2021-a-comprehensively-tight-ana.tldr: A tight analysis shows how the spectral gap and target accuracy jointly govern gradient descent convergence for PCA.

paragraphs: Robotic reinforcement learning can struggle because exploring a continuous action space requires discovering useful behavior through many possible control choices. This paper changes the interface between the learning algorithm and the robot. The authors manually define a library of robot action primitives, called RAPS, whose arguments are learned by the reinforcement learning policy.

These primitives give the policy structured actions to work with while retaining flexibility through their parameters. The abstract describes them as expressive, straightforward to implement, and transferable across robots, tasks, and environments. The central idea is that improving the action interface itself can make exploration more effective, alongside improvements to optimization or exploration algorithms.

The empirical study covers challenging tasks in three distinct domains, using image observations and sparse rewards delivered at the end. Across the underlying reinforcement learning algorithms studied, RAPS substantially improves learning efficiency and task performance. It also significantly outperforms prior methods that learn skills from offline expert data. These findings support manually specified, parameterized actions as a practical way to improve robotic learning.
neurips-2021-accelerating-robotic-reinfo.tldr: Manually specified action primitives with learned parameters substantially improve robotic reinforcement learning in the reported experiments.

paragraphs: A causal quantity can sometimes be identified using several available formulas. This paper asks how an investigator should choose among them when the goal is a precise estimate. The selection criterion is asymptotic variance: the authors seek the formula with the lowest such variance while using as few samples as possible to identify it.

The setting assumes that data collection can be changed online in response to observations already obtained. The authors formulate formula selection as a best-arm-identification bandit problem. Here, an arm is judged by the quality of the estimate it will produce, replacing the usual objective of choosing the arm with the lowest loss.

A key contribution is finite-sample confidence bounds for estimated asymptotic variances that account for potentially complex nuisance-function estimation. The authors adapt LUCB and Successive Elimination to use these bounds. They provide sample-complexity upper bounds and experiments on artificial data. The work connects adaptive data collection with selecting an efficient causal estimator, while keeping the target explicitly tied to asymptotic precision.
neurips-2021-asymptotically-best-causal-.tldr: A bandit framework adaptively collects data to identify the available causal formula with the lowest asymptotic variance.

paragraphs: Online learning usually studies how much worse an algorithm can perform than the best fixed action chosen after seeing all outcomes. This paper examines the opposite direction: how much better can the algorithm do? A best-case lower bound on regret limits that improvement, helping characterize how an algorithm adapts to favorable sequences.

The authors develop a general method for Follow The Regularized Leader algorithms with time-varying regularizers. They show that best-case lower bounds have the same order as existing upper regret bounds across several settings, including fixed and decreasing learning rates, timeless methods, and adaptive gradient methods. These results describe both sides of the algorithm’s possible performance relative to the fixed-action comparator.

The linearized version of FTRL behaves differently: it can achieve negative regret growing linearly in magnitude. The paper also fully characterizes best-case sequences for two experts with binary losses. Beyond adaptivity, the motivation includes fairness, because such lower bounds are useful in constructing decision-theoretic online learning algorithms satisfying a notion of group fairness.
neurips-2021-best-case-lower-bounds-in-o.tldr: Best-case regret bounds reveal how much FTRL algorithms can outperform the best fixed action and distinguish them from linearized FTRL.

paragraphs: This paper addresses recovering a tensor from noisy observations when some entries may be missing. Its proposed model represents the underlying signal through a series of structured sign tensors. This provides a nonparametric approach to completion that can address both low-rank and high-rank signals, expanding the range of tensors the method can estimate.

The sign representation includes several established tensor models as special cases, including CP, Tucker, single-index models, and structured tensors with repeating entries. The authors prove that estimating the tensor can be reduced to solving a sequence of structured classification problems. Their reduction lets existing low-rank tensor algorithms contribute to the more challenging task of estimating high-rank signals.

The theoretical results include bounds on excess risk, estimation error, and sample complexity. These establish quantitative support for the reduction rather than relying only on a new representation. Experiments on human brain connectivity and topic-mining datasets show improvements over previous methods. The findings suggest that useful structure can reside in a tensor’s sign-series representation even when low rank alone is insufficient.
neurips-2021-beyond-the-signs-nonparamet.tldr: Structured sign series turn noisy tensor completion into classification tasks that can handle both low-rank and high-rank signals.

paragraphs: This paper examines classification performance on the worst-off samples, rather than focusing only on average accuracy. A common objective is Conditional Value at Risk, or CVaR, which averages losses in the unfavorable tail. The authors identify a specific obstacle when classifiers are deterministic and evaluation uses zero-one loss.

Under those conditions, a classifier minimizing average zero-one loss also minimizes CVaR zero-one loss. Consequently, changing to the CVaR objective does not by itself provide the hoped-for benefit without additional assumptions. The authors turn to randomized classifiers, for which the average-loss and CVaR minimizers need not coincide. This creates room for improving tail performance through the choice of objective.

They develop Boosted CVaR Classification from a direct connection between CVaR and LPBoost, then introduce an algorithm called α-AdaLPBoost. On four benchmark datasets, it achieves higher tail performance than deterministic training methods. The contribution combines a precise negative result with a constructive alternative: randomization makes CVaR optimization potentially useful in the classification setting studied.
neurips-2021-boosted-cvar-classification.tldr: Randomized boosted classifiers make CVaR optimization useful for improving tail performance where deterministic zero-one classification faces an obstacle.

paragraphs: Graph neural networks repeatedly combine each node’s representation with information from its neighbors. With many layers, this process can make node embeddings increasingly alike, a problem known as over-smoothing. The paper studies this bottleneck through the Dirichlet energy of node embeddings and uses that analysis to guide the design of deeper networks.

The resulting framework, Energetic Graph Neural Networks, places lower and upper constraints on Dirichlet energy at each layer. Instead of selecting architectural changes solely through heuristics or borrowing techniques from convolutional networks, the approach uses an explicit energy-based principle to regulate the representations as they pass through the network. The intended effect is to avoid the collapse associated with repeated aggregation.

The authors report state-of-the-art experimental performance using deep layers. This supports the usefulness of their proposed training principle in the evaluated setting. The main contribution is both analytical and architectural: a way to describe the depth bottleneck and a corresponding framework that incorporates layer-by-layer constraints aimed at controlling it.
neurips-2021-dirichlet-energy-constraine.tldr: Energetic Graph Neural Networks constrain layer-wise Dirichlet energy to counter over-smoothing and improve deep GNN performance.

paragraphs: Real-world graphs can reflect interactions among several hidden factors. Learning a single holistic representation may mix those influences together, making the result harder to interpret and less useful for later tasks. This paper introduces Disentangled Graph Contrastive Learning, or DGCL, to learn graph-level representations that separate latent aspects using self-supervision.

DGCL first identifies latent factors in an input graph and derives a factorized representation. Each component is intended to describe an aspect associated with a particular factor. The method then applies a factor-wise contrastive discrimination objective, encouraging the components to independently capture expressive information from different factors. Separating the learning objective by factor is central to the proposed approach.

Experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets show that DGCL outperforms several state-of-the-art baselines. These results support the value of learning differentiated components within a graph representation. The paper’s contribution is a self-supervised method for addressing entanglement directly, connecting the structure of the learned representation with an objective designed to preserve information about distinct latent influences.
neurips-2021-disentangled-contrastive-le.tldr: DGCL uses factor-wise contrastive learning to build self-supervised graph representations that separate latent influences.

paragraphs: Local treatment effects concern people who comply with the treatment they are assigned. Much existing work summarizes these effects with an average. This paper instead studies estimating their density, which provides information about the distribution of effects beyond a single central value. The change in target is the main motivation for the proposed methods.

The authors develop two approaches. One uses smooth kernel functions to estimate the density. The other projects the density onto a finite-dimensional class of candidate densities. These provide distinct ways to represent the distribution, and the paper derives double or debiased machine learning estimators for both approaches.

The analysis establishes asymptotic convergence rates and shows robustness to biases in estimated nuisance functions, the auxiliary functions needed by the estimation procedure. This matters because errors in those supporting estimates can affect the final treatment-effect estimate. Synthetic data and the 401(k) dataset illustrate the methods. Together, the contributions extend the estimation focus from an average local effect to a more informative distributional description.
neurips-2021-double-machine-learning-den.tldr: Two debiased machine learning approaches estimate the density of local treatment effects and provide robustness to nuisance-estimation biases.

paragraphs: Some graph neighborhoods cannot be distinguished by standard message-passing graph neural networks. DropGNN addresses this expressive limitation by running a GNN several times on randomly altered versions of the input graph. In each run, nodes are dropped independently at random, and the outputs of the runs are combined into a final result.

The important contribution is that these repeated random changes can provide distinguishing information unavailable to the standard framework. The authors prove that DropGNNs can separate various neighborhoods that message-passing GNNs cannot. They also derive bounds on how many runs are needed to obtain a reliable distribution of dropouts and establish additional properties of the method’s expressive power and limits.

Experiments validate the theoretical findings about expressiveness, while established GNN benchmarks show competitive performance. The results give node dropout a role beyond simply modifying training: aggregating multiple dropout runs becomes part of the representational mechanism. The claim is an increase in distinguishable graph structures, supported by theory and experiments, rather than an assertion that every graph can be distinguished.
neurips-2021-dropgnn-random-dropouts-inc.tldr: Combining GNN runs with random node dropouts can distinguish graph neighborhoods that standard message passing cannot.

paragraphs: Lagrangian and Hamiltonian neural networks encode physical structure into learned dynamics, including energy conservation. The differential-equation approaches discussed in this paper do not allow state discontinuities, restricting their ability to describe contacts and collisions. Those events are central to physical systems such as legged robots and manipulators.

The authors introduce a differentiable contact model that covers frictionless and frictional interactions as well as elastic and inelastic contacts. It also supports inequality constraints, including joint-angle limits. Incorporating this model extends the networks so that contact properties and other system properties can be learned simultaneously from data.

The framework is demonstrated on challenging two-dimensional and three-dimensional systems with different friction and restitution coefficients. These demonstrations address the kinds of interactions that motivated the extension. Because the learned contact model is differentiable, the resulting dynamics can serve as a differentiable physics simulator for gradient-based downstream tasks such as planning and control. The contribution connects structured dynamics learning with physical events involving abrupt changes.
neurips-2021-extending-lagrangian-and-ha.tldr: A differentiable contact model extends Lagrangian and Hamiltonian networks to learn collisions, friction, and constrained physical dynamics.

paragraphs: Exploration in a learning system can impose costs unevenly across groups. This paper studies how to share those costs in a multi-armed bandit setting where each time step is associated with one group from a finite collection. It evaluates a group’s benefit through the reduction in its regret compared with learning on its own.

The authors use the Nash bargaining solution to choose among the incremental utilities achievable by learning policies. They derive policies that realize this bargaining solution, giving a formal way to balance the benefits of shared learning across groups. This makes the comparison with independent learning central to the fairness objective.

Their analysis shows that the resulting price of fairness is limited, while regret-optimal policies can be arbitrarily unfair under generic conditions. Thus, optimizing aggregate learning performance can leave substantial disparities unresolved. A contextual-bandit case study on warfarin dosing examines exploration costs across racial and age groups. The study complements the theoretical account of how bargaining can shape the distribution of learning benefits.
neurips-2021-fair-exploration-via-axioma.tldr: Nash bargaining yields bandit policies that distribute exploration benefits fairly with a limited price of fairness.

paragraphs: Few-shot segmentation seeks to adapt to new object classes using only a few examples. This paper argues that summarizing support images into semantic prototypes leaves useful pixel-level information unused. Its Cycle-Consistent Transformer, or CyCTR, transfers support information through relationships between individual support and query image features.

CyCTR uses cross-attention to aggregate support features into the query representation. However, some support pixels may be irrelevant, so unrestricted attention can bias the query features. The proposed cycle-consistent attention mechanism filters potentially harmful support features and encourages attention to the most informative pixels. The method therefore combines richer access to the examples with a mechanism for selecting relevant information.

The authors report improvements over previous state-of-the-art methods on the few-shot segmentation benchmarks evaluated. For five-shot segmentation, they obtain 66.6% mIoU on Pascal-5^i and 45.6% on COCO-20^i, with reported gains of 4.6% and 7.1%, respectively. These findings support using detailed pixel relationships while controlling which support features contribute to each query prediction.
neurips-2021-few-shot-segmentation-via-c.tldr: CyCTR improves few-shot segmentation by transferring pixel-level support features through cycle-consistent attention that filters irrelevant information.

paragraphs: This paper approaches Bayesian inference by approximating a distribution over functions. Its Functional Variational Inference method minimizes a divergence between a variational distribution and the posterior process directly in function space. The object being approximated is therefore the posterior distribution of possible functions, which is the central focus of the proposed inference procedure.

The authors introduce Stochastic Process Generators as a flexible family of distributions for this approximation. Their design makes the functional evidence lower bound efficiently estimable using analytic solutions together with mini-batch sampling. This connection between a flexible variational family and a tractable training objective is what makes the proposed function-space approach computationally usable.

FVI can be applied to stochastic-process priors when random function samples from those priors are available. That sampling requirement specifies the stated scope of applicability. Across several experimental tasks, the authors report consistently better performance than the compared weight-space and function-space variational inference methods. The results support the effectiveness of the generator-based approximation in the settings studied.
neurips-2021-functional-variational-infe.tldr: Stochastic Process Generators enable efficient variational inference directly over functions when prior function samples are available.

paragraphs: Recurrent neural networks are used to investigate computations in biological neural circuits, but their behavior can depend on modeling choices. This paper asks which computational features persist across learning rules and task designs. Such persistence would make those features more plausible candidates for neurobiological mechanisms, without establishing that they occur in biological systems.

The authors train large populations of RNNs using different commonly used learning rules on neuroscience-inspired decision-making tasks. For relatively complex tasks, they find that attractor topology remains unchanged across learning rules, while representational geometry varies. Thus, the organization of the network’s attractors can be stable even when the arrangement of its internal representations depends on training.

Task design produces another distinction. For simple tasks, attractor topology depends on input noise, but this dependence disappears as task complexity increases in the study. The findings suggest that RNN dynamics can be robust to learning-rule choices while remaining sensitive to how tasks are constructed. They also identify simpler tasks as particularly sensitive to the input-noise choice.
neurips-2021-learning-rule-influences-re.tldr: In the studied decision tasks, learning rules alter RNN representations while attractor topology is more stable, especially for complex tasks.

paragraphs: Predicting a likely route requires more than producing plausible road choices along the way. The authors find that a significant portion of routes recommended by existing methods fail to reach their destinations. They also identify a generalization problem: transductive methods cannot recommend routes when they encounter previously unseen roads at inference time.

NeuroMLR addresses these problems with an inductive generative model learned from historical trajectories. Its conditional distributions use the current location, the destination, and real-time traffic conditions as explanatory factors. The model combines Lipschitz embedding with graph convolutional networks to learn these distributions, bringing road-network structure into the route-generation process.

Experiments on real-world datasets show significant accuracy improvements over the state of the art. The authors also report substantially better generalization to unseen data and a much higher likelihood that recommended routes reach the destination. These findings address both the quality of route predictions and their practical completion. Destination arrival remains a probabilistic improvement in the stated results, rather than a guaranteed property.
neurips-2021-neuromlr-robust-reliable-ro.tldr: NeuroMLR learns an inductive route model that improves accuracy, unseen-data generalization, and the likelihood of reaching the destination.

paragraphs: This paper studies robust optimal transport formulations that relax the usual marginal constraints using Kullback–Leibler divergence. Its focus is computational: how much work is needed to approximate the optimal cost to a desired accuracy? The authors analyze Sinkhorn-based algorithms for this relaxed transport problem.

They show that the optimal cost can be approximated in Õ(n²/ε) time, where n counts distribution support points and ε is the desired error. They also investigate a fixed-support robust barycenter problem for m discrete distributions, each with at most n support points. For this problem, they develop an approximation algorithm based on iterative Bregman projections.

For the specific case of two distributions, the barycenter algorithm approximates the optimal value in Õ(mn²/ε) time. Its dependence on accuracy improves on the cited Õ(mn²/ε²) complexity for iterative Bregman projections applied to Wasserstein barycenters. The two-distribution qualification is essential to that stated bound. The contribution establishes computational guarantees for both robust transport costs and this particular robust barycenter setting.
neurips-2021-on-robust-optimal-transport.tldr: The paper establishes efficient approximation bounds for KL-relaxed optimal transport and, with two distributions, robust barycenter computation.

paragraphs: Optical Processing Units are low-power photonic chips built for large-scale random projections. Earlier work used them to train deep networks through Direct Feedback Alignment, an alternative to backpropagation. This paper investigates how the intrinsic noise in those optical projections can also support a differentially private training mechanism.

The authors construct a private DFA mechanism around that noise and provide a theoretical analysis of its adaptive privacy behavior. The analysis tracks how optical projection noise propagates through the learning process and establishes a differential privacy guarantee. This connects a physical property of the computation to a formal property of the resulting training procedure.

Experiments demonstrate solid end-task performance for the proposed learning method. The stated outcome is therefore a combination of provable privacy and useful empirical learning behavior. The privacy claim comes from the analyzed mechanism and the way it handles noise; the contribution is the deliberate incorporation of hardware noise into private training. It gives optical random projections an additional function beyond their existing role in implementing DFA.
neurips-2021-photonic-differential-priva.tldr: An analyzed Direct Feedback Alignment mechanism uses optical projection noise to provide differential privacy while retaining solid task performance.

paragraphs: Object detectors are commonly evaluated using Average Precision, which combines localization and classification performance. Because AP is not differentiable, training often uses separate differentiable objectives for those tasks. This creates a mismatch between what the detector optimizes and how it is evaluated, which can reduce performance.

The paper proposes Parameterized AP Loss to make the choice of approximation searchable. Parameterized functions replace the non-differentiable components of the AP calculation, placing different approximations within one unified formula. An automatic search algorithm then selects the parameters. This makes the construction of the training objective part of the optimization process instead of relying entirely on a manually designed surrogate.

Experiments on COCO cover RetinaNet, Faster R-CNN, and Deformable DETR. Across those detectors, the proposed loss consistently outperforms the handcrafted losses used for comparison. These results support searching over AP approximations as a useful way to align training with evaluation. The empirical breadth across three detectors is part of the evidence for the approach’s usefulness.
neurips-2021-searching-parameterized-ap-.tldr: Automatically searching a parameterized approximation to Average Precision improves detection performance over compared handcrafted losses on COCO.

paragraphs: SOLQ is an end-to-end instance segmentation framework built on DETR. It represents each object with a learned query that jointly captures its class, location, and mask. The central design is a unified vector representation through which classification, bounding-box regression, and mask encoding are learned together.

To train the mask component, the method compresses raw spatial masks into codes and uses those codes to supervise the predicted mask vectors. At inference time, the inverse coding process converts each predicted vector directly into a spatial mask. This links the compact query representation to the pixel-level output needed for segmentation.

The authors report state-of-the-art segmentation performance, exceeding most existing approaches in their evaluation. They also find that jointly learning the unified query representation can substantially improve DETR’s detection performance. This means the combined representation contributes beyond the added mask output: its joint training also benefits object detection. The paper presents SOLQ as a strong potential baseline for Transformer-based instance segmentation.
neurips-2021-solq-segmenting-objects-by-.tldr: SOLQ jointly learns object class, box, and compressed mask representations through unified queries, improving segmentation and DETR detection.

paragraphs: ODE-Nets connect neural networks with dynamical systems by treating depth continuously. This paper represents their depth-dependent weights as linear combinations of basis functions. Viewing weights as functions in this way makes transformations such as function projection available and provides the foundation for a new ODE block that supports stateful layers.

One benefit is the ability to incorporate meaningful continuous-in-depth batch normalization. Another is weight compression through a change of basis. The latter can be performed without retraining, allowing the weight representation to be altered after learning while retaining near state-of-the-art performance in the reported results. The method therefore connects the functional description of weights with both architectural support and compression.

The authors demonstrate the stateful block on image classification with convolutional units and sentence tagging with Transformer encoder units. They report state-of-the-art performance with the normalization-enabled design, while compression reduces inference time and memory use. These findings show how the same basis-function perspective can support stateful computation and provide a practical means of reducing deployment costs.
neurips-2021-stateful-ode-nets-using-bas.tldr: Basis-function representations enable stateful ODE blocks with batch normalization and weight compression without retraining.

paragraphs: Test-time training adapts a model using self-supervision on incoming data, aiming to handle distribution shifts. This paper shows that adaptation can instead hurt performance when the shift is severe. It investigates that failure mode and introduces TTT++, which adds feature alignment to help regulate the adaptation process.

The method summarizes features offline and matches feature moments online, allowing adaptation to use training-derived information without revisiting the training data. Batch-queue decoupling supports robust moment estimates even when online batches are small. These components make the alignment strategy usable in a setting where incoming data and batch sizes constrain adaptation.

Given aligned feature distributions, the authors theoretically analyze post-adaptation performance. That conditional analysis motivates more informative self-supervision through contrastive learning for visual recognition. TTT++ outperforms state-of-the-art methods by significant margins on several benchmarks. The results suggest that retaining useful information beyond model parameters can improve test-time adaptation, while the paper’s opening finding makes clear that self-supervised adaptation alone need not be beneficial.
neurips-2021-ttt-when-does-self-supervis.tldr: TTT++ combines feature alignment and contrastive self-supervision to improve test-time adaptation, which can otherwise deteriorate under severe shifts.

paragraphs: The geometry of a representation space affects which structures it can naturally describe. This paper considers ultrahyperbolic spaces, drawn from pseudo-Riemannian geometry and generalizing both hyperbolic and spherical geometries. Earlier work had used these spaces for a particular type of nonparametric embedding, motivating the question of how to learn parametric models there.

A central difficulty is that not every pair of ultrahyperbolic points is connected by a geodesic. This creates an obstacle for constructing neural networks in the space. The paper introduces a method for learning parametric ultrahyperbolic models, addressing the transition from learning individual embeddings to learning a model that operates within this geometry.

The authors evaluate their approach on graph classification and node classification, with experiments demonstrating its relevance to both tasks. The contribution expands the geometric settings available for neural representation learning. Its stated empirical result is that the method is useful in those classification settings; the abstract does not claim that ultrahyperbolic geometry is uniformly preferable to other representation spaces.
neurips-2021-ultrahyperbolic-neural-netw.tldr: The paper enables parametric neural models in ultrahyperbolic space and demonstrates their relevance to graph and node classification.

paragraphs: A supervised learning task may be trained through a convex surrogate whose predictions are vectors. This paper asks how small those vectors can be while still allowing a surrogate consistent with the target task. The minimum such size is called the convex consistency dimension, and lower bounds establish dimensions below which a suitable surrogate cannot exist.

The authors introduce a tool called d-flats, based on property elicitation, for proving these lower bounds. The approach unifies reasoning across continuous and discrete prediction problems. Its value lies in providing a shared way to analyze the dimensional requirements of surrogate losses across domains that had used different techniques.

Applied to risk measures, the tool produces a new lower bound and resolves an existing open question. In discrete prediction, it recovers and sometimes strengthens earlier bounds based on feasible subspace dimension. These are structural results about what convex surrogate formulations require. They help characterize the possible prediction spaces before a particular optimization algorithm or model is chosen.
neurips-2021-unifying-lower-bounds-on-pr.tldr: The d-flats tool unifies and strengthens lower bounds on the prediction dimension required by consistent convex surrogates.

paragraphs: Human feedback in reinforcement learning can communicate more than whether an action was good or bad. This paper studies adding visual explanations: a trainer evaluates queried state-action pairs and marks relevant features in the associated images. The goal is to use that extra information to guide what the learning model represents.

The proposed method, EXPAND, converts those annotations into context-aware data augmentation. It perturbs features identified as irrelevant while preserving the task-relevant information indicated by the trainer. This encourages the model to encode the features that matter for the feedback, making the explanation part of the learning procedure rather than merely an additional annotation.

The evaluation covers Pixel-Taxi and four Atari games, examining performance and sample efficiency. EXPAND significantly outperforms compared methods that adapt human-explanation techniques from supervised learning, as well as human-in-the-loop reinforcement learning baselines using evaluative feedback alone. The findings support a concrete way to make richer human guidance useful: use visual relevance annotations to determine which image variations the model should learn from.
neurips-2021-widening-the-pipeline-in-hu.tldr: EXPAND uses human visual explanations to guide image augmentation and improve learning from evaluative reinforcement-learning feedback.
